question: According to the Vaughan-Williams classification, amiodarone is primarily classified as a Class III antiarrhythmic. What is the primary mechanism of Class III agents?

answers.text: Potassium channel blockade, prolonging the action potential duration and effective refractory period

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Class III agents (amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide, dofetilide) block cardiac K+ channels (especially IKr), prolonging repolarisation and the effective refractory period. This terminates re-entry circuits that depend on differential refractoriness.

answers.text: Sodium channel blockade, slowing phase 0 depolarisation and conduction velocity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Sodium channel blockade is the mechanism of Class I agents (quinidine, lidocaine, flecainide). Class III agents act on potassium channels.

answers.text: Calcium channel blockade, slowing AV nodal conduction

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. AV nodal calcium channel blockade is the mechanism of Class IV agents (verapamil, diltiazem). Amiodarone does have some calcium channel blocking properties, but its primary class III mechanism is K+ channel blockade.

answers.text: Beta-adrenergic receptor blockade, reducing sympathetic drive to the SA node

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Beta-adrenergic receptor blockade is the mechanism of Class II agents (metoprolol, atenolol). Amiodarone has some beta-blocking activity as well, but it is classified Class III based on its dominant K+ channel blockade.

overallFeedback.feedback: Class III antiarrhythmics block potassium channels (particularly IKr), prolonging action potential duration and effective refractory period. This is the primary mechanism of amiodarone, sotalol, ibutilide, and dofetilide.

Correct. Class III = K+ channel blockade → prolonged APD and ERP → anti-re-entry. Amiodarone is the most clinically used Class III agent but also possesses Class I, II, and IV properties ('broad-spectrum' antiarrhythmic).
